_link.title: I can describe the specialised cells of the pancreas, thyroid, thymus and gonads and the hormones they produce

toLevel2.stem: Which specialised cells in the pancreas produce insulin?

options.text: Beta cells
options.explanation: Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans produce and secrete insulin, which decreases blood glucose levels.

options.text: Alpha cells
options.explanation: Alpha cells in the islets of Langerhans produce glucagon, which increases blood glucose levels.

options.text: Leydig cells
options.explanation: Leydig cells are found in the testes and produce testosterone, not insulin.

options.text: Follicular cells
options.explanation: Follicular cells are found in the thyroid and produce thyroxine, not insulin.

toLevel2.stem: What hormone is produced by parafollicular cells in the thyroid gland?

options.text: Calcitonin
options.explanation: Parafollicular cells (also called C cells) produce calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium levels.

options.text: Thyroxine
options.explanation: Thyroxine is produced by follicular cells, not parafollicular cells.

options.text: Thymosin
options.explanation: Thymosin is produced by epithelial cells in the thymus, not by thyroid cells.

options.text: PTH
options.explanation: PTH (parathyroid hormone) is produced by the parathyroid glands, not the thyroid's parafollicular cells.

toLevel2.stem: Which cells in the testes produce testosterone?

options.text: Leydig cells
options.explanation: Leydig cells are specialised cells in the testes that are stimulated by LH and FSH to produce and secrete testosterone.

options.text: Granulosa cells
options.explanation: Granulosa cells are found in the ovaries and produce oestrogen, not testosterone.

options.text: Beta cells
options.explanation: Beta cells are found in the pancreas and produce insulin.

options.text: Epithelial cells
options.explanation: Epithelial cells in the thymus produce thymosin. Leydig cells in the testes produce testosterone.

toLevel2.stem: What is the function of thymosin released by the thymus?

options.text: It stimulates the maturation of immature T-cells into functional immune cells
options.explanation: Thymosin is released by epithelial cells in the thymus when immature T-cells arrive from bone marrow, causing them to mature before entering the bloodstream.

options.text: It increases metabolic rate in all body tissues
options.explanation: Increasing metabolic rate is the function of thyroxine from the thyroid, not thymosin from the thymus.

options.text: It lowers blood calcium levels
options.explanation: Lowering blood calcium is the function of calcitonin from the thyroid's parafollicular cells.

options.text: It stimulates development of male sex characteristics
options.explanation: Male sex characteristics are stimulated by testosterone from Leydig cells in the testes.

toLevel2.stem: Which specialised cells in the ovaries produce oestrogen?

options.text: Granulosa cells
options.explanation: Granulosa cells in the ovaries contribute to oestrogen production. Granulosa lutein cells produce progesterone.

options.text: Leydig cells
options.explanation: Leydig cells are found in the testes and produce testosterone, not oestrogen.

options.text: Follicular cells
options.explanation: Follicular cells are in the thyroid gland and produce thyroxine. Granulosa cells in the ovaries produce oestrogen.

options.text: Alpha cells
options.explanation: Alpha cells are in the pancreas and produce glucagon. Granulosa cells in the ovaries produce oestrogen.

toLevel2.stem: Alpha cells in the islets of Langerhans produce glucagon, which increases blood glucose levels.
toLevel2.explanation: Alpha cells in the pancreatic islets of Langerhans produce glucagon. This hormone stimulates the liver to release stored glucose, raising blood glucose levels.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. Alpha cells do produce glucagon, and glucagon does increase blood glucose levels.

toLevel2.stem: Follicular cells in the thyroid produce calcitonin.
toLevel2.explanation: Follicular cells produce thyroxine. Calcitonin is produced by parafollicular cells in the thyroid.

options.text: True
options.explanation: This is false. Follicular cells produce thyroxine. It is the parafollicular cells that produce calcitonin.

toLevel2.stem: In the pancreas, {{blank:1}} cells produce insulin and {{blank:2}} cells produce glucagon.
The thymus contains specialised {{blank:1}} cells that release {{blank:2}} to stimulate T-cell maturation.
{{blank:1}} cells in the testes produce testosterone, while {{blank:2}} cells in the ovaries produce oestrogen.

toLevel3.stem: Why does the pancreas need two different cell types (alpha and beta) in the islets of Langerhans?

options.text: Because alpha cells produce glucagon to raise blood glucose and beta cells produce insulin to lower it, providing antagonistic control
options.explanation: Having two specialised cell types allows the pancreas to both raise and lower blood glucose, enabling precise homeostatic regulation through antagonistic hormone action.

options.text: Because alpha and beta cells produce the same hormone at different rates
options.explanation: Alpha and beta cells produce different hormones (glucagon and insulin respectively), not the same hormone at different rates.

options.text: Because one cell type handles digestion and the other handles hormone production
options.explanation: Both alpha and beta cells are endocrine (hormone-producing). Digestive enzymes are produced by the exocrine tissue of the pancreas, which is separate from the islets.

options.text: Because beta cells only function during the day and alpha cells at night
options.explanation: Both cell types function continuously based on blood glucose levels, not a day-night cycle.

toLevel3.stem: How does the dual function of the thyroid (follicular and parafollicular cells) contribute to body regulation?

options.text: Follicular cells regulate metabolic rate via thyroxine, while parafollicular cells regulate blood calcium via calcitonin — two separate regulatory functions
options.explanation: The thyroid houses two distinct cell types with different targets: thyroxine acts on all tissues to control metabolism, while calcitonin acts on bones and kidneys to lower blood calcium.

options.text: Both cell types produce thyroxine but in different concentrations
options.explanation: Only follicular cells produce thyroxine. Parafollicular cells produce calcitonin, a completely different hormone with a different function.

options.text: Follicular cells produce hormones and parafollicular cells destroy them
options.explanation: Both cell types produce hormones. Parafollicular cells produce calcitonin; they do not destroy other hormones.

options.text: The two cell types work together to produce a single combined hormone
options.explanation: Each cell type produces a distinct hormone independently. Thyroxine and calcitonin are separate molecules with separate functions.

toLevel3.stem: Why is it significant that sex hormones (testosterone and oestrogen) are produced in both males and females?

options.text: The difference between sexes is the relative amount of each hormone, not the presence or absence of one
options.explanation: Males have about seven times more testosterone than females, while females produce significantly more oestrogen. Both hormones are present in both sexes — it is the ratio that determines sex characteristics.

options.text: Both sexes produce identical amounts of testosterone and oestrogen
options.explanation: The amounts differ significantly between sexes. Males produce much more testosterone, and females produce much more oestrogen.

options.text: Sex hormones in the opposite sex serve no biological function
options.explanation: Both hormones serve functions in both sexes. For example, some testosterone is converted to oestrogen in males, playing a role in male fertility and sexual function.

options.text: This only occurs during puberty and stops in adulthood
options.explanation: Both sexes produce both hormones throughout life, not just during puberty. The levels change with age but both hormones remain present.

toLevel3.stem: What is the relationship between the thymus, thymosin and the immune system?

options.text: Epithelial cells in the thymus release thymosin when immature T-cells arrive from bone marrow, causing them to mature into functional immune cells
options.explanation: Immature T-cells migrate from bone marrow to the thymus. Their arrival triggers thymosin release from epithelial cells, which stimulates the T-cells to mature before they enter the bloodstream.

options.text: The thymus produces antibodies that are distributed by thymosin
options.explanation: The thymus does not produce antibodies. Thymosin stimulates T-cell maturation. Antibodies are produced by B-cells, which mature in the bone marrow.

options.text: Thymosin destroys pathogens directly in the bloodstream
options.explanation: Thymosin does not destroy pathogens. It is a hormone that stimulates immature T-cells to mature into functional immune cells that can then fight pathogens.

options.text: T-cells produce thymosin to signal the thymus to make more immune cells
options.explanation: Thymosin is produced by epithelial cells in the thymus, not by T-cells. The T-cells are the recipients of thymosin's action, not its producers.

toLevel3.stem: Why are sex hormones classified as lipid-based rather than protein-based?

options.text: Because they are derived from cholesterol, are hydrophobic, and can diffuse through the plasma membrane to bind intracellular receptors
options.explanation: Testosterone, oestrogen and progesterone are steroid hormones built from cholesterol. Their hydrophobic nature allows them to pass through the phospholipid bilayer and bind to receptors in the cytosol.

options.text: Because they are made of amino acid chains that fold into lipid-like structures
options.explanation: Amino acid chains form protein-based hormones. Sex hormones are derived from cholesterol, a lipid molecule, not from amino acids.

options.text: Because they are stored in fat cells before being released
options.explanation: Sex hormones are produced by specialised gland cells (Leydig cells, granulosa cells), not stored in fat cells. Their lipid classification comes from their chemical structure.

options.text: Because they only act on fatty tissues in the body
options.explanation: Sex hormones act on many tissue types including gonads, skin, muscle and bone. Their lipid classification refers to their chemical structure, not their targets.

toLevel3.stem: Explain the difference between the exocrine and endocrine tissue of the pancreas.

options.text: Exocrine tissue produces digestive enzymes released via ducts, while endocrine tissue (islets of Langerhans) produces hormones released into the blood
options.explanation: The pancreas has dual functions: exocrine cells release pancreatic juice via the pancreatic duct into the duodenum, while the islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon directly into the bloodstream.

options.text: Exocrine tissue produces insulin and endocrine tissue produces glucagon
options.explanation: Both insulin and glucagon are endocrine products from the islets of Langerhans. Exocrine tissue produces digestive enzymes.

options.text: Exocrine and endocrine tissue both produce hormones but release them at different times
options.explanation: Exocrine tissue produces digestive enzymes, not hormones. Only the endocrine tissue (islets of Langerhans) produces hormones.

options.text: Exocrine tissue releases products into the blood while endocrine tissue releases them into ducts
options.explanation: This is reversed. Exocrine means secretion into ducts; endocrine means secretion into the blood.

toLevel3.stem: Testosterone is only produced in males and oestrogen is only produced in females.
toLevel3.explanation: Both hormones are produced in both sexes. The difference is the amount: males produce about seven times more testosterone than females, and females produce significantly more oestrogen than males.

options.text: True
options.explanation: This is false. Both testosterone and oestrogen are produced in both males and females, but in different amounts.

toLevel3.stem: The pancreas has both exocrine tissue that produces {{blank:1}} and endocrine tissue (islets of Langerhans) that produces {{blank:2}}.
Sex hormones are {{blank:1}}-based, meaning they can diffuse through the plasma membrane and bind to {{blank:2}} receptors.
Immature T-cells migrate from the {{blank:1}} to the thymus, where {{blank:2}} stimulates their maturation.

toLevel4.stem: In Type 1 diabetes, immune cells destroy the beta cells of the pancreas. What direct effect does this have on blood glucose regulation?

options.text: The body cannot produce insulin, so blood glucose levels remain dangerously high after meals
options.explanation: Without beta cells, no insulin is produced. Glucose cannot be taken up by liver, muscle and fat cells, causing blood glucose to rise uncontrollably after eating.

options.text: The body cannot produce glucagon, so blood glucose drops too low
options.explanation: Glucagon is produced by alpha cells, not beta cells. In Type 1 diabetes, alpha cells are unaffected. The problem is loss of insulin from destroyed beta cells.

options.text: Both insulin and glucagon production stop completely
options.explanation: Only beta cells are destroyed in Type 1 diabetes. Alpha cells continue to produce glucagon. The specific loss is insulin production.

options.text: The pancreas compensates by using exocrine tissue to produce insulin
options.explanation: Exocrine tissue produces digestive enzymes and cannot switch to producing insulin. The loss of beta cells cannot be compensated for by other pancreatic tissue.

toLevel4.stem: A patient has their thymus removed in childhood. Predict the long-term effect on their immune system.

options.text: T-cell production would be impaired because thymosin is no longer available to stimulate maturation of immature T-cells
options.explanation: Without the thymus and its epithelial cells releasing thymosin, immature T-cells from bone marrow cannot be matured. This leads to a weakened adaptive immune response over time.

options.text: The immune system would be completely unaffected
options.explanation: The thymus plays a critical role in T-cell maturation. Without it, the supply of new mature T-cells is compromised, weakening immune defence.

options.text: Blood glucose regulation would be disrupted
options.explanation: Blood glucose is regulated by the pancreas (insulin and glucagon), not the thymus. Thymus removal affects T-cell maturation and immune function.

options.text: The patient would produce excess antibodies as compensation
options.explanation: Antibodies are produced by B-cells, not T-cells. Thymus removal affects T-cell development specifically and does not cause B-cell overactivation.

toLevel4.stem: A researcher treats thyroid cells with a substance that selectively destroys parafollicular cells but not follicular cells. Which function would be lost?

options.text: The ability to lower blood calcium levels via calcitonin
options.explanation: Parafollicular cells produce calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium. Destroying them removes this function while leaving thyroxine production by follicular cells intact.

options.text: The ability to regulate metabolic rate via thyroxine
options.explanation: Thyroxine is produced by follicular cells, which are unaffected. Only the calcitonin-producing parafollicular cells are destroyed.

options.text: Both calcium regulation and metabolic rate control
options.explanation: Only parafollicular cells are destroyed, so only calcitonin production is lost. Follicular cells continue producing thyroxine normally.

options.text: The ability to produce thymosin for immune function
options.explanation: Thymosin is produced by the thymus, not the thyroid. Thyroid cell destruction has no effect on thymosin production.

toLevel4.stem: An athlete uses anabolic steroids (synthetic testosterone). How would this affect their Leydig cells over time?

options.text: Leydig cells would reduce testosterone production because negative feedback from synthetic testosterone suppresses LH and FSH
options.explanation: High synthetic testosterone triggers negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, reducing LH and FSH. Without LH stimulation, Leydig cells decrease their natural testosterone production and may atrophy.

options.text: Leydig cells would increase testosterone production to match the synthetic levels
options.explanation: Negative feedback suppresses LH, which stimulates Leydig cells. Less LH means less stimulation and reduced natural testosterone production.

options.text: Leydig cells would be unaffected because synthetic hormones do not interact with natural cells
options.explanation: Synthetic testosterone participates in the same feedback loops as natural testosterone, suppressing the signals that stimulate Leydig cells.

options.text: Leydig cells would switch to producing oestrogen instead
options.explanation: While some testosterone is normally converted to oestrogen, Leydig cells do not switch their primary function. They produce less testosterone due to reduced LH stimulation.

toLevel4.stem: A blood test shows a patient has normal insulin levels but elevated blood glucose. Based on cell-specific knowledge, what is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Target cells have become resistant to insulin, so glucose is not being absorbed despite normal beta cell function
options.explanation: This describes Type 2 diabetes: beta cells still produce insulin, but liver, muscle and fat cells respond poorly. Blood glucose stays high even though insulin is present.

options.text: Alpha cells are producing too much insulin
options.explanation: Alpha cells produce glucagon, not insulin. Insulin is produced by beta cells. Also, the question states insulin levels are normal.

options.text: Beta cells have been destroyed by the immune system
options.explanation: If beta cells were destroyed (Type 1 diabetes), insulin levels would be very low or absent. The question states insulin levels are normal.

options.text: Follicular cells in the thyroid are interfering with glucose regulation
options.explanation: Thyroid follicular cells produce thyroxine for metabolic rate, not for direct blood glucose regulation. The issue is insulin resistance at target cells.

toLevel4.stem: During puberty, increased release of LH and FSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the gonads. What specific cells are activated in males versus females?

options.text: In males, Leydig cells are stimulated to produce testosterone; in females, granulosa cells are stimulated to produce oestrogen
options.explanation: LH and FSH act on the specific hormone-producing cells of each gonad: Leydig cells in the testes for testosterone and granulosa cells in the ovaries for oestrogen.

options.text: In both sexes, beta cells are activated to produce sex hormones
options.explanation: Beta cells are in the pancreas and produce insulin. Leydig cells (testes) and granulosa cells (ovaries) are the specialised gonadal cells.

options.text: In males, granulosa cells produce testosterone; in females, Leydig cells produce oestrogen
options.explanation: This is reversed. Leydig cells are in the testes (testosterone), and granulosa cells are in the ovaries (oestrogen).

options.text: In both sexes, follicular cells are activated to produce sex hormones
options.explanation: Follicular cells are in the thyroid and produce thyroxine. Gonadal cells are Leydig cells (testes) and granulosa cells (ovaries).

toLevel4.stem: A patient is diagnosed with a condition that impairs granulosa cell function in the ovaries. What hormonal changes would you expect?

options.text: Reduced oestrogen production, potentially affecting female sex characteristics and the menstrual cycle
options.explanation: Granulosa cells produce oestrogen. Impaired function reduces oestrogen output, which can disrupt the development and maintenance of female sex characteristics and menstrual cycle regulation.

options.text: Reduced testosterone production affecting male sex characteristics
options.explanation: Granulosa cells are in the ovaries and produce oestrogen, not testosterone. Testosterone is produced by Leydig cells in the testes.

options.text: Reduced insulin production affecting blood glucose levels
options.explanation: Insulin is produced by beta cells in the pancreas. Granulosa cell impairment affects oestrogen production in the ovaries.

options.text: Reduced calcitonin production affecting blood calcium levels
options.explanation: Calcitonin is produced by parafollicular cells in the thyroid. Granulosa cells in the ovaries produce oestrogen.

toLevel4.stem: In Type 1 diabetes, immune cells destroy {{blank:1}} cells, eliminating the body's ability to produce {{blank:2}}.
Destroying only parafollicular cells would eliminate {{blank:1}} production while leaving {{blank:2}} production by follicular cells unaffected.
Without the thymus, immature T-cells from bone marrow cannot receive {{blank:1}} and therefore cannot {{blank:2}} into functional immune cells.

toLevel5.stem: Compare the consequences of destroying all alpha cells versus all beta cells in the pancreas. Which would be more immediately life-threatening?

options.text: Destroying beta cells would be more immediately dangerous because uncontrolled high blood glucose leads to diabetic ketoacidosis, which can be fatal within days
options.explanation: Without insulin, cells cannot absorb glucose, leading to the body breaking down fats for energy and producing toxic ketones. Without glucagon (alpha cells destroyed), the body can still maintain some glucose from dietary intake, making it less immediately critical.

options.text: Destroying alpha cells would be more dangerous because blood glucose would crash immediately
options.explanation: Without glucagon, blood glucose regulation is impaired during fasting, but dietary glucose intake and other hormones (like cortisol) provide some compensation. Beta cell loss causes more acute, life-threatening consequences.

options.text: Both would be equally dangerous because insulin and glucagon are equally important
options.explanation: While both are important, the acute consequences differ. Beta cell destruction leads to diabetic ketoacidosis within days, while alpha cell destruction can be partially compensated by dietary glucose and other hormones.

options.text: Neither would be life-threatening because the liver can regulate glucose independently
options.explanation: The liver responds to insulin and glucagon signals. Without beta cells and insulin, glucose regulation fails dangerously. The liver cannot independently maintain glucose homeostasis.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that the thymus is unimportant because it shrinks with age. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: The claim is flawed because the thymus is critical during childhood for establishing the T-cell repertoire, and mature T-cells continue to function long after the thymus shrinks
options.explanation: The thymus is most active during childhood, when it matures T-cells that then persist for years. Even after thymus involution, the immune system retains its T-cell diversity from earlier maturation.

options.text: The claim is correct because a shrinking organ has no biological value
options.explanation: Thymus shrinkage (involution) is a normal process. The thymus has already accomplished its key role of establishing the T-cell population during youth.

options.text: The claim is correct because adults do not need T-cells
options.explanation: Adults absolutely need T-cells for immune defence. The T-cells matured during youth continue to function throughout adulthood, even after the thymus shrinks.

options.text: The claim is flawed because the thymus actually grows larger with age
options.explanation: The thymus does shrink with age (involution). The claim is flawed not because of this factual error, but because thymus importance is based on its critical early-life role, not its current size.

toLevel5.stem: The pancreas has both exocrine and endocrine tissue. Analyse why a disease that damages the entire pancreas would have more widespread effects than one that only targets the islets of Langerhans.

options.text: Whole-pancreas damage disrupts both digestion (exocrine enzymes) and blood glucose regulation (endocrine hormones), while islet-only damage affects only glucose regulation
options.explanation: The exocrine tissue produces enzymes essential for digesting carbohydrates, proteins and fats in the duodenum. Losing this plus the endocrine function (insulin/glucagon) would impair both digestion and metabolic regulation simultaneously.

options.text: Both would have identical effects because the islets produce all pancreatic products
options.explanation: The islets only produce hormones. Exocrine tissue produces digestive enzymes. Whole-pancreas damage eliminates both functions.

options.text: Islet-only damage would be worse because hormones are more important than enzymes
options.explanation: Both functions are essential. Without exocrine enzymes, nutrient digestion and absorption would fail, leading to severe malnutrition alongside glucose dysregulation.

options.text: Whole-pancreas damage would only affect digestion, not hormone production
options.explanation: Whole-pancreas damage affects everything: exocrine (digestive enzymes) and endocrine (insulin and glucagon). Both functions would be lost.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate why knowing the specific cell type affected is important for treating endocrine disorders.

options.text: Identifying the affected cell type determines which hormone is deficient and guides targeted replacement therapy or treatment strategies
options.explanation: For example, knowing that Type 1 diabetes involves beta cell destruction tells clinicians to replace insulin specifically. Knowing that follicular cells are affected guides thyroxine replacement. Cell-level diagnosis enables precise treatment.

options.text: Cell type identification is unnecessary because all endocrine disorders are treated the same way
options.explanation: Different cell types produce different hormones with different functions. Treatment must be targeted: insulin for beta cell loss, thyroxine for follicular cell dysfunction, etc.

options.text: Cell type identification is only useful for research, not clinical treatment
options.explanation: Clinical treatment directly depends on knowing which cells and hormones are affected. This guides drug choice, dosage and monitoring strategies.

options.text: Knowing the cell type only matters for surgical treatments, not hormone therapy
options.explanation: Cell type identification is critical for both surgical and pharmacological approaches. Hormone replacement therapy must match the specific hormone lost from the specific cell type.

toLevel5.stem: In some males, testosterone produced by Leydig cells is converted to oestrogen. Analyse why this conversion is biologically important rather than being a flaw.

options.text: Oestrogen plays an important role in male fertility and sexual function, so this conversion serves a necessary regulatory purpose
options.explanation: Males require some oestrogen for bone density, fertility and brain function. Converting testosterone to oestrogen ensures males have appropriate levels of both hormones for full physiological function.

options.text: It is a biological flaw that evolution has not corrected
options.explanation: Testosterone-to-oestrogen conversion is a conserved and beneficial process. It is maintained because males need oestrogen for important physiological functions.

options.text: The conversion only occurs in diseased individuals
options.explanation: Testosterone-to-oestrogen conversion is a normal physiological process in healthy males, not a sign of disease.

options.text: It eliminates excess testosterone to prevent overproduction
options.explanation: While conversion does reduce testosterone levels, its primary purpose is to produce oestrogen that males need for fertility and other functions, not simply to dispose of excess testosterone.

toLevel5.stem: A new treatment for Type 1 diabetes involves transplanting islets of Langerhans from a donor. Evaluate the potential advantages and limitations of this approach.

options.text: It could restore both insulin and glucagon production from functioning beta and alpha cells, but the transplanted cells may be attacked by the same immune response that caused the original disease
options.explanation: Transplanted islets can provide natural glucose regulation with both insulin and glucagon. However, since Type 1 diabetes involves immune destruction of beta cells, the transplanted cells face the same immune attack unless immunosuppression is used.

options.text: It would only restore insulin production because glucagon is not important
options.explanation: Islet transplants include both alpha and beta cells. Glucagon is important for preventing dangerous blood glucose drops. Both hormones being restored is a significant advantage.

options.text: It would cure the disease permanently with no risk of recurrence
options.explanation: The underlying autoimmune cause of Type 1 diabetes persists. Without immunosuppression, the immune system may attack the transplanted beta cells, causing recurrence.

options.text: It would fail because transplanted cells cannot produce hormones outside the original pancreas
options.explanation: Islet cells can function when transplanted to other sites. They respond to blood glucose and secrete hormones into the bloodstream regardless of their location.

toLevel5.stem: Compare how thymosin and thyroxine interact with their target cells, given that thymosin is protein-based and thyroxine is also protein-based.

options.text: Both bind to membrane receptors on their target cells because both are protein-based and hydrophilic, but they trigger different intracellular responses in different cell types
options.explanation: As protein-based hormones, both thymosin and thyroxine bind to surface receptors. Thymosin triggers T-cell maturation in immune cells, while thyroxine triggers increased metabolic rate across all tissues — different responses from the same binding mechanism.

options.text: Thymosin uses membrane receptors but thyroxine uses intracellular receptors because they target different cells
options.explanation: Receptor location depends on hormone chemistry (protein vs lipid), not target cell type. Both thymosin and thyroxine are protein-based, so both use membrane receptors.

options.text: Both enter their target cells and directly alter gene expression
options.explanation: Protein-based hormones cannot cross the plasma membrane. Both thymosin and thyroxine signal from the cell surface via membrane receptor binding.

options.text: Neither interacts with receptors because they are too small
options.explanation: All hormones interact with receptors. Size does not determine whether a hormone uses receptors — all hormones bind to specific complementary receptors on or in target cells.

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that because the thyroid has two cell types producing different hormones, it is actually two separate glands. Evaluate this reasoning.

options.text: The reasoning is flawed; having multiple specialised cell types within one organ is common in biology and does not make the thyroid two separate glands
options.explanation: The pancreas also has multiple tissue types (exocrine and endocrine). Multiple cell types with different functions within one anatomical structure is a normal feature of organ specialisation, not evidence of being separate glands.

options.text: The reasoning is correct because different cell types always belong to different organs
options.explanation: Most organs contain multiple cell types. The stomach has chief cells, parietal cells, goblet cells and G cells — yet it is one organ. Multiple cell types within a gland is the norm.

options.text: The reasoning is correct because follicular and parafollicular cells have different embryological origins
options.explanation: Even if cell types have different origins, they form part of the same anatomical gland. The thyroid is defined as a single gland based on its structure and location, regardless of cell type origins.

options.text: The reasoning is flawed only because both cell types produce the same type of product
options.explanation: Follicular cells produce thyroxine (metabolic rate) and parafollicular cells produce calcitonin (calcium regulation) — different products. The reasoning is flawed because having different cell types in one organ is normal, not because they produce the same product.

toLevel5.stem: Destroying beta cells causes more immediately life-threatening consequences than destroying alpha cells because without {{blank:1}}, cells cannot absorb glucose and the body produces toxic {{blank:2}}.
Islet transplants for Type 1 diabetes risk failure because the same {{blank:1}} that destroyed the original beta cells may attack the {{blank:2}} cells.
